The Roman Republic was born out of the ashes of the Monarchy in 509 BC, a pivotal moment traditionally marked by the expulsion of the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, by the patrician Lucius Junius Brutus and the legendary hero Lucretia. This revolution established a mixed constitution that divided power among three major components: the two annually elected Consuls, who held supreme military and civil authority (imperium) but served only one-year terms to prevent the accumulation of personal power, and the Senate, an advisory body composed of former magistrates and prominent patricians that controlled finances and foreign policy. Crucially, the creation of the Comitia Centuriata and later the Comitia Tributa allowed for a limited form of popular sovereignty, although in the early years, political rights were heavily skewed toward the wealthy patrician class. This new system was cemented by the creation of the Twelve Tables in 451–450 BC, the first written codification of Roman law, which established the principle that laws must be public and applied equally to all citizens, thereby providing the legal foundation upon which the Republic would build its complex civic identity and legal traditions for centuries to come.

In an eager execution model, every kernel launch involves the CPU interacting with the driver to encode command buffers, which introduces significant latency, especially for small or numerous kernels. This process is serial and can bottleneck performance if the GPU becomes idle waiting for the next command. By contrast, a CUDA Graph captures a sequence of kernel launches, memory copies, and events into a single, pre-compiled data structure. When this graph is instantiated, the entire workflow is uploaded to the GPU as a single unit. Consequently, the GPU can schedule these operations with much lower CPU interference, allowing for tighter pipelining and reduced idle time between dependent tasks.

The second major advantage stems from the graph's ability to optimize scheduling at the GPU level. While eager launching relies on the host to determine the order and dependencies of operations, the CUDA runtime can analyze the graph structure to identify independent branches of the workflow. Eager kernel launching incurs significant CPU overhead for every individual operation. When a program launches thousands of small CUDA kernels sequentially, the CPU must repeatedly interact with the GPU driver, validate arguments, manage synchronization points, and issue launch commands. This CPU-GPU communication often becomes the bottleneck, especially for inference workloads with small tensors or complex control flow, as the GPU spends a considerable amount of time idle waiting for the next instruction while the CPU is busy preparing it.

A CUDA Graph mitigates this by capturing a sequence of these kernel launches into a single dependency graph on the CPU side. Instead of issuing commands one by one, the entire graph is uploaded to the GPU memory as a compact structure. Once the graph is instantiated, replaying it involves only a single driver call to execute the pre-compiled stream of operations. This shifts the scheduling overhead from the CPU to the GPU’s hardware scheduler, drastically reducing API call latency and allowing the GPU to keep its execution units fully utilized by minimizing idle gaps between small kernels.
